title: How to Welcome a Stranger
excerpt: Scripture keeps insisting we welcome the stranger because we were strangers once. Hospitality to outsiders is not a personality trait. It is an obedience.
body:
The writer of Hebrews tells us not to neglect hospitality to strangers, because some have entertained angels without knowing it. The Greek word behind hospitality means love of the stranger. Not love of the guest who is already a friend. Love of the one you do not know and have no reason to love yet. That is the harder and the more biblical command.

We live in a time built to avoid strangers. We order so we do not have to speak. We pull into garages so we do not have to wave. We have arranged our days to need no one and meet no one new. And then we wonder why our faith feels private and our lives feel thin. The stranger is not an interruption to the Christian life. The stranger is one of its appointed places.

## Why the stranger keeps appearing in Scripture

Israel was commanded to love the foreigner because they had been foreigners in Egypt. The memory of their own strangeness was meant to make them merciful. The same logic runs through the whole story. We welcome the stranger because we were strangers to God and were welcomed in anyway. If you have received that welcome, withholding it from the person new to your town or your church is a contradiction of the gospel you claim.

## Notice who is new

Welcome begins with noticing, and noticing is a discipline because our default is to scan for the familiar. The new family at church standing alone after the service. The neighbor who just moved in and knows no one. The coworker eating lunch by themselves. The new kid your child has not mentioned. These people are visible only to the person looking for them, and most of us are not looking. Train your eyes. Before you leave a room, ask who here came in alone.

## Make the first move and absorb the awkwardness

The stranger will almost never come to you. The weight of crossing the gap belongs to the one who already belongs, and that is you. So you go first. You say your name. You ask theirs. You absorb the small awkwardness of the opening so they do not have to. This is a real cost, and it is the whole point. Welcome means you carry the discomfort so the stranger can feel ease. Jesus carried infinitely more so that we, strangers and enemies, could be brought near.

## Move them from stranger to guest

A greeting is a start, not a welcome. Welcome moves the stranger toward your table and your life. "Come sit with us." "Let me introduce you to a few people." "Come over Sunday and eat with my family." Each step shortens the distance. The goal is not a polite acknowledgment. The goal is that the stranger stops being a stranger. That takes more than a handshake. It takes an invitation into your actual life, which costs your time and your privacy, which is exactly why it means something.

## Welcome the ones you would not choose

The test of hospitality is the stranger you would not have picked. The one who is hard to talk to, dressed wrong, smells of trouble, holds opinions you find offensive. Welcoming the impressive stranger is just networking. Welcoming the inconvenient one is obedience. Jesus drew to himself precisely the people the respectable crowd kept at a distance, and the respectable crowd never forgave him for it. Your welcome will be tested by who you are willing to seat at your table.

## Let it cost you

Real welcome is inconvenient. It eats your evening, complicates your schedule, brings someone unpredictable into your space. If your hospitality costs you nothing, it is probably not hospitality. It is decoration. The angels in the old stories were entertained by people who set a real table and gave up a real evening, not by people who waved from a distance. Welcome with your front door open, not just your hand.

## This week

Find one person who is new, to your church, your street, your workplace, and make the first move. Learn their name and offer them a next step beyond the greeting, even a small one: a seat beside you, an introduction, a meal. Carry the awkwardness so they do not have to. You may be welcoming an angel. You will certainly be welcoming someone the same way you were once welcomed, when you were the stranger God brought near.
